solution:
**(C)** macromolecules

The chapter says all living organisms have three basic types of macromolecules, which are polymers of simple subunits: polysaccharides, polypeptides and polynucleotides are the polymers of monosaccharides, amino acids and nucleotides respectively. Sugars, amino acids and nucleotides are themselves the micromolecules (monomers), and bioelements are the chemical elements such as carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen from which all of these are built.

**(D)** each of these

A glycosidic bond links a sugar to another group through the sugar's first carbon. In a disaccharide it holds the two monosaccharide units together, as the chapter states, and a polysaccharide is a long chain of such units joined by repeated condensation, so it is full of glycosidic bonds. In a nucleoside the nitrogenous base is attached to the first carbon of the sugar, and this link is an N-glycosidic bond.

[Note: the chapter does not name the base-sugar link in a nucleoside; standard biology gives that it is an N-glycosidic bond.]

**(D)** none of these

In proteins, amino acids are linked by peptide bonds, which join the carboxyl group of one amino acid to the amino group of the next. Peptide bond is not among the choices. Hydrogen bonds hold the helix or pleated sheet of the secondary structure, disulphide bonds help fold the chain into its tertiary structure, and glycosidic bonds join sugars, so none of them joins amino acids in the chain.

More than one option is correct as printed, so no single letter can be keyed.

Phospholipids are the main lipids of the cell membrane: the chapter says they contribute to the formation of the cell membrane and arrange as a bilayer with polar heads outward and non-polar tails inward. This is the answer the question most likely intends. But sphingomyelin is itself a membrane phospholipid, and cholesterol is a membrane lipid too (it is drawn in the fluid mosaic model in the Cell Structure chapter), so those two options are also true. Only isoprenoids are not a general membrane lipid.

[Note: the chapter does not mention sphingomyelin; standard biology gives that sphingomyelin is a phospholipid of animal cell membranes, especially the myelin sheath.]

**(A)** Arachidonic

Linoleic, linolenic and arachidonic acids are the polyunsaturated fatty acids traditionally called essential fatty acids, because the body cannot make them in sufficient amounts and must get them from the diet. Oleic acid is unsaturated but the body can make it, and palmitic and stearic acids are saturated fatty acids found in all animal and plant fats.

[Note: the chapter does not list the essential fatty acids; standard biology gives linoleic, linolenic and arachidonic acids.]

**(C)** conjugated

A conjugated protein is a simple protein united with a non-protein prosthetic group. The chapter gives haemoglobin as the example: globin is the protein and the iron-containing pigment haem is the prosthetic group. A simple protein yields only amino acids on hydrolysis, a derived protein is a breakdown product such as a peptone, and complex is not one of the three structural classes.

**(B)** holoenzyme

The protein part of an enzyme is the apoenzyme, and it is inactive on its own. When its non-protein part (an inorganic metal ion or an organic or metallo-organic group) is bound to it, the complete active enzyme is called the holoenzyme. An isoenzyme is a different molecular form of an enzyme catalysing the same reaction, and a denatured enzyme is one whose shape has been destroyed by heat or pH.

**(B)** Enzyme has higher affinity towards substrate

Km is the substrate concentration at which the reaction runs at half its maximum velocity (Vmax/2); the stem's "Km = Vmax/2" is a loose way of saying this. The chapter states that a low Km value indicates a strong affinity between enzyme and substrate, because half the enzyme molecules are already bound at a low substrate concentration. A low Km does not stop product formation, and it says nothing about every active site being saturated.
